with the service has degraded — requests feel slow or are failing
for them. The on-call team needs you to investigate.

abnormal_metrics_sum.parquet, normal_metrics.parquet,
normal_traces.parquet, normal_logs.parquet.

Walk the telemetry to identify which endpoints / services are
actually affected, then determine the root cause(s) of the
degradation.


Code has surveyed this case's telemetry; the survey follows. Use it as a starting point and check it: it may miss what matters.

content.text: No restarts, no pod changes and no network errors, so this looks like an in-process or HTTP-layer fault. Frontend's own time rose from 1.4 to 5.8 ms, so I'll break frontend and its callees down by operation.

input.query: SELECT 'abn' p, service_name, span_name, count(*) n, round(quantile_cont(duration,0.5)/1e6,2) p50, round(quantile_cont(duration,0.95)/1e6,2) p95 FROM abnormal_traces WHERE service_name IN ('frontend','search','reservation','profile','rate') GROUP BY 1,2,3 UNION ALL SELECT 'norm', service_name, span_name, count(*), round(quantile_cont(duration,0.5)/1e6,2), round(quantile_cont(duration,0.95)/1e6,2) FROM normal_traces WHERE service_name IN ('frontend','search','reservation','profile','rate') GROUP BY 1,2,3 ORDER BY 2,3,1

content.text: Several spans show a p50 of 0 ms in the abnormal period (rate's memcached call, reservation's memcached calls), which suggests calls failing fast or returning empty. I'll check the time profile of these spans to see where it starts.

input.query: SELECT service_name, span_name, count(*) n, sum(CASE WHEN duration < 50000 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) tiny, round(avg(duration)/1e6,3) avg_ms, min(time) t0, max(time) t1 FROM abnormal_traces WHERE service_name IN ('rate','reservation','search','profile','user','geo','recommendation','attractions') GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 1,2

content.text: About half of the memcached spans in rate and reservation are near-zero in the abnormal period. I'll compare that fraction with the normal period and check the per-minute timing.

input.query: SELECT service_name, span_name, count(*) n, sum(CASE WHEN duration < 50000 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) tiny, round(avg(duration)/1e6,3) avg_ms FROM normal_traces WHERE span_name LIKE 'memcached%' GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 1,2

SELECT service_name, span_name, date_trunc('minute', time) m, count(*) n, sum(CASE WHEN duration < 50000 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) tiny FROM abnormal_traces WHERE span_name LIKE 'memcached%' GROUP BY 1,2,3 ORDER BY 1,2,3

content.text: The memcached spans have the same ~50% near-zero share in both periods, so the earlier p50 shifts are just a mix artifact and not a fault. Next I'll look at the gauge metrics, where the survey found the largest shifts (search container CPU usage).

input.query: SELECT metric, service_name, round(avg(CASE WHEN src='a' THEN value END),3) abn_avg, round(avg(CASE WHEN src='n' THEN value END),3) norm_avg FROM (SELECT 'a' src, * FROM abnormal_metrics UNION ALL SELECT 'n', * FROM normal_metrics) GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 1,2

content.text: Search's CPU jumped from about 0.006 to 2.7 cores, the only large gauge change. I'll look at how that CPU and memory moved over time, and whether anything else in the search pod changed.

input.query: SELECT date_trunc('minute', time) m, metric, round(avg(value),3) v, count(*) n FROM abnormal_metrics WHERE service_name='search' AND metric IN ('container.cpu.usage','container.memory.usage','k8s.pod.memory.page_faults','k8s.container.restarts') GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 2,1

SELECT metric, round(avg(value),3) v, count(*) n, round(min(value),3) mn, round(max(value),3) mx FROM normal_metrics WHERE service_name='search' AND metric IN ('container.cpu.usage','container.memory.usage') GROUP BY 1

content.text: Search's container CPU sits at about 2.85 cores from the first abnormal minute onward, roughly 400 times its normal level. Next I'll check whether that is reflected in the request flow, using per-minute counts and the search-to-downstream latencies.

input.query: SELECT 'abn' p, date_trunc('minute', time) m, service_name, count(*) n, round(quantile_cont(duration,0.95)/1e6,2) p95 FROM abnormal_traces WHERE service_name IN ('frontend','search','rate','geo') AND span_name IN ('search.Search/Nearby','rate.Rate/GetRates','geo.Geo/Nearby','HTTP /hotels') GROUP BY 1,2,3 UNION ALL SELECT 'norm', date_trunc('minute', time) m, service_name, count(*), round(quantile_cont(duration,0.95)/1e6,2) FROM normal_traces WHERE service_name IN ('frontend','search','rate','geo') AND span_name IN ('search.Search/Nearby','rate.Rate/GetRates','geo.Geo/Nearby','HTTP /hotels') GROUP BY 1,2,3 ORDER BY 3,1,2

content.text: Latencies are flat across the abnormal window while span volume drops in every service, so the volume drop looks like reduced upstream traffic rather than a failure. To see whether search's CPU saturation leaks into its own time, I'll compare self-time per span with a parent/child join.

input.query: SELECT column_name FROM (DESCRIBE abnormal_traces)

WITH s AS (SELECT 'a' p, trace_id, span_id, parent_span_id, service_name, span_name, attr_span_kind, duration FROM abnormal_traces UNION ALL SELECT 'n', trace_id, span_id, parent_span_id, service_name, span_name, attr_span_kind, duration FROM normal_traces), c AS (SELECT p, trace_id, parent_span_id pid, sum(duration) cd, count(*) cn FROM s GROUP BY 1,2,3) SELECT s.service_name, s.span_name, s.p, count(*) n, round(quantile_cont(s.duration - coalesce(c.cd,0),0.5)/1e6,3) self_p50, round(quantile_cont(s.duration - coalesce(c.cd,0),0.95)/1e6,3) self_p95, round(avg(s.duration)/1e6,3) avg_total FROM s LEFT JOIN c ON s.p=c.p AND s.trace_id=c.trace_id AND s.span_id=c.pid WHERE s.service_name IN ('search','frontend','rate','reservation') AND s.attr_span_kind='SPAN_KIND_SERVER' GROUP BY 1,2,3 ORDER BY 1,2,3
SELECT attr_span_kind, service_name, count(*) n FROM abnormal_traces GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 2 LIMIT 40

WITH s AS (SELECT 'a' p, trace_id, span_id, parent_span_id, service_name, span_name, attr_span_kind, duration FROM abnormal_traces UNION ALL SELECT 'n', trace_id, span_id, parent_span_id, service_name, span_name, attr_span_kind, duration FROM normal_traces), c AS (SELECT p, trace_id, parent_span_id pid, sum(duration) cd FROM s GROUP BY 1,2,3) SELECT s.service_name, s.attr_span_kind, s.span_name, s.p, count(*) n, round(quantile_cont(s.duration - coalesce(c.cd,0),0.5)/1e6,3) self_p50, round(quantile_cont(s.duration - coalesce(c.cd,0),0.95)/1e6,3) self_p95, round(quantile_cont(s.duration,0.5)/1e6,3) tot_p50, round(quantile_cont(s.duration,0.95)/1e6,3) tot_p95 FROM s LEFT JOIN c ON s.p=c.p AND s.trace_id=c.trace_id AND s.span_id=c.pid WHERE s.service_name IN ('search','frontend','reservation') GROUP BY 1,2,3,4 ORDER BY 1,2,3,4

content.text: Self-times match between periods in every service, so the trace latency picture is flat. The only real anomaly so far is search's CPU. Next I'll check the log templates for anything that differs between periods.

content.text:
**Verdict: the evidence supports CPU saturation of `search`, but not clearly `container_cpu_saturated`. The telemetry can't separate container from process here, and nothing shows that the saturation slowed the service.**

**What holds up**
- The CPU rise is real and sustained. `container.cpu.usage` averages 0.006 cores normally (0.005–0.007 across 22 samples) and 2.74 cores in the incident (2.86 max, 45 samples). `k8s.pod.cpu.usage` matches it, so the pod and container agree.
- It is not a restart. Uptime rises steadily (11,971–12,266 s), there are no new pods, and readiness is unchanged.
- The rise is not start-up. It runs through the whole window, not just the first minutes.

**What argues against `container_cpu_saturated` as a slowdown**
- `search`'s own work did not slow. Its Server `search.Search/Nearby` p50 fell from about 5.5 ms to about 1.1–3.3 ms over the window, and its own-time p95 moved only from 6.0 to 6.7 ms. A pinned container would normally stretch every span, and it does not.
- The call graph shows no slowdown on search's outgoing calls. `geo` p50 is flat at 0.4 ms. `rate` p50 went from 3.7 to 2.7 ms. The Client spans around search are not stretched.
- Work fell while CPU rose. Frontend spans dropped from 1,843 to 573 a minute, `search` spans from 584 to 204, and calls to `search` from about 162 to 3.6 a minute. CPU went up about 460× while throughput fell about 65%. That is roughly 2,000× more CPU per request. A saturated service would serve less work per CPU core, not more. This looks like a burn with no matching work, not a service starved of CPU.

**What the telemetry cannot settle**
- Container and process CPU are indistinguishable here. There are no `jvm.*` metrics for `search`, and no `container.cpu` limit or throttling metric, so I cannot check whether the 2.86-core ceiling is a cgroup limit or whether one process is pinned.
- The ceiling (max 2.86, flat across minutes) hints at a cap, which would favour container-level saturation. But that is inference, not a measured limit, and a single busy process can also plateau. Per the boundary rule, `process_cpu_saturated` is the alternative to keep open.

**Confidence**
- CPU-saturation family for `search`: moderate. The CPU surge is clear, and the drop in work with no slowdown argues against it being a load-driven saturation.
